title: Stablecoins
generatedFrom: frontend/src/content/stablecoins (run: cd frontend && npm run chat-context)
overview:
TOPIC: Stablecoins, on Banking Rails to Digital Finance, an authored reference for banking and payments practitioners. Facts as publicly reported at 18 November 2026.

THESIS: A stablecoin moves a claim on an issuer across a ledger quickly. A payment is complete only when the payee holds what it asked for: local currency it can spend from its bank account, or dollar tokens in its own wallet. Funding, conversion, cash-out, reachability, screening, liquidity and reconciliation decide whether a stablecoin route wins, loses or complements other rails. The FSB said in November 2026 that "faster payment initiation alone is not sufficient".

1. A CLAIM, NOT A COIN. A stablecoin is a token that represents a claim on its issuer, which holds reserves (Treasury bills, repo, money-market funds, cash) and redeems at $1 for holders it has onboarded, on its terms. Tokens are minted when money comes in and burned when it goes out. Two prices: the redemption price ($1 from the issuer, less fees) and the market price. Holders who can redeem keep the market price near $1 by buying below $1 and redeeming, or minting at $1 and selling above it. If redemption is closed (weekend, pause) or reserves are doubted, the price can slip. Redemption rules: MiCA lets e-money token holders redeem at par at any time; the OCC's GENIUS Act rule requires redemption within two business days from 18 January 2027; FCA rules (from 25 October 2027) require redemption by the next business day after checks; the Bank of England expects systemic sterling coins to redeem within 24 hours. Tether's minimum is $100,000, with a fee of the greater of $1,000 or 0.1%. History: USDC fell to about $0.88 in March 2023 when $3.3bn of its reserves were at the failed Silicon Valley Bank, and recovered when depositors were protected; the algorithmic TerraUSD collapsed in May 2022 and a US jury later found its issuer liable for fraud ($4.5bn in penalties). A tokenised deposit is the bank's own deposit as a token (JPMorgan calls JPM Coin a deposit token, "not a stablecoin"); a bank-issued stablecoin is backed by segregated reserves rather than the bank's deposit book (SG-FORGE, a Societe Generale subsidiary, issues EURCV and USDCV under MiCA; SoFi Bank issues SoFiUSD itself). The PRA expects UK banks to offer retail digital money as deposits and to issue stablecoins only from a separate, insolvency-remote, distinctly branded entity (PRA letter of 18 May 2026, read via a law-firm summary).

2. WHO USES THEM. Crypto trading is still the main use (BIS 2026). Over 98% are US-dollar. Supply was $286.4bn on 17 November 2026, down from a $312.9bn peak on 17 May; USDT was $175.2bn (61%) and USDC $69.2bn (24%). Gross on-chain transfers in 2025 were $28tn to $35tn depending on the source; genuine payments were about $390bn by McKinsey and Artemis's estimate, of which about $226bn business-to-business; the BIS gives a similar figure for transfers net of moves between a holder's own wallets, citing Chainalysis and Visa data. BIS research found treating every on-chain transfer as a payment misclassifies about six in ten. Chainalysis counts $220bn of cross-border transfers it can attribute in the year to June 2026 (vendor lower bound; not all are payments). Visa's payments volume was $14.2tn in fiscal 2025, for scale.

3. FOLLOW £1,000 (interactive): four routes for one invoice. See the scene notes. No published source prices a £1,000 UK-outbound payment. IMF WP/26/230 (30 Oct 2026) priced USD 200 stablecoin "sandwich" transfers across 270 corridors: 2.18% average with the cheapest ramps, 3.04% median-priced, 4.07% dearest, 1.54% at USD 5,000; the blockchain leg was under a quarter of the cost; in about a third of comparable corridors the cheapest traditional provider was cheaper; speed, counterparty risk and onboarding were excluded. The global average cost of sending USD 200 was 6.2% in Q1 2026 across traditional providers, and 3.0% for the three cheapest (FSB). The FSB says the G20's 2027 targets are unlikely to be met. Big-bank retail wires can carry FX margins of 2-4% (BIS WP 1385, small sample). Swift says 75% of its payments reach the beneficiary bank within 10 minutes (operator data); the FSB finds 57% of wholesale cross-border payments are credited to the end customer within an hour. Stablecoin routes tend to win on hours, reach where correspondent banks have withdrawn (if a licensed off-ramp exists), payees who want dollars, and firms' own treasury moves. They tend to lose where instant domestic systems and payment firms serve a corridor well, in thinly traded currencies, where refunds or fraud reimbursement matter, and where two conversions add cost.

4. PICK THE PAYMENT MODEL (interactive selector). Separate three questions: which token (whose liability), which route (how value travels), who earns what (partnership economics). Circle's payments network describes itself as an orchestration layer; its operating entity says it holds no funds, while its managed service does. Its $58bn "annualised volume" (30 Oct 2026) is a 30-day run-rate scaled to a year.

5. LIQUIDITY (interactive control room). The token runs 24/7; money at either end doesn't. Someone must prefund stablecoin inventory and local-currency payout floats. Minting and redemption follow US banking days and cut-offs (Circle settles wires same day before cut-off and typically pays out next business day; Tether says redemptions can take several days). Market makers fill gaps at a spread that widens under stress; flows in the other direction allow netting (Circle nets mint and redeem orders hourly); credit can bridge gaps but no issuer was found minting before money arrives (issuance is cash in advance, which the BIS says limits elasticity).

6. ACROSS CHAINS (interactive failure lab). USDC is on 39 blockchains (two redemption-only); Circle's burn-and-mint protocol links 31. USDT (61% of supply) has no issuer-run equivalent: it relies on third-party mechanisms such as USDT0 or on exchanges. Four ways across: the issuer's burn and mint (Circle CCTP: minting is idempotent, each signed confirmation can be used once; burning again is a second transfer; a Fast option credits the destination before source finality, backed by a Circle-funded allowance; confirmations expire after about 24 hours and can be reissued; CCTP V1 is paused on 1 December 2026), a lock-and-mint bridge (the wrapped token is a claim on the bridge; bridges were 64% of the $3.1bn stolen from DeFi in 2022; KelpDAO lost about $292m in April 2026 through a single-verifier bridge setup), a liquidity pool, or a provider paying from its own inventory (counterparty risk). Ethereum blocks take about 15 minutes to finalise; optimistic-rollup withdrawals wait about seven days. Keep the payment in transit on the books until the destination is final; look up an unknown outcome before acting.

7. KEEPING CRIME OUT (interactive). Same duties as any payment. The UK Travel Rule has applied since 1 September 2023; since 30 June 2026 full originator data is needed on cross-border transfers of £800 or more. FATF (July 2026): 83% of surveyed jurisdictions have Travel Rule laws but 60% of those have taken no supervisory action. UK treatment of self-custody wallets is risk-based; the EU requires ownership checks above EUR 1,000. The bank's role decides its duties: sending from its own custody makes it a cryptoasset business with Travel Rule duties, and if requested information about a self-custody wallet never arrives it must not make the transfer; paying money to a licensed provider that sends the tokens leaves the Travel Rule with that provider while the bank keeps its customer, sanctions and reporting duties. Stablecoins were 84% of illicit crypto volume in 2025 per Chainalysis, driven by flows to sanctioned entities; TRM puts illicit activity at about 1.2% of attributed volume. Issuer freezes are not a backstop: in the October 2026 Binance theft (about $6bn), hundreds of millions in stablecoins were swapped before issuers froze the rest.

8. WHO EARNS WHAT (interactive comparison). Issuers earn reserve income; holders get no interest from issuers (banned under MiCA now, GENIUS from January 2027, UK rules from October 2027); some platforms pass part of their share back as rewards, which is the open question in the US. In Q3 2026 Circle earned $658m of reserve income and paid $409m in distribution and transaction costs; Coinbase takes half of residual income plus all income on USDC held on Coinbase. Paxos offers Global Dollar Network partners up to 100% of returns on USDG on their platforms. Open USD went live on 30 September 2026, issued by Bridge (part of Stripe), under a company founded by Coinbase, Mastercard, Shopify, Stripe and Visa; supply about $961m on 17 November 2026; it says most reserve income goes to participants but no payouts or fees are published, so that is a stated design, not evidence. Issuer-by-issuer detail is on the site's "Stablecoin market structure" topic.

9. DOLLAR STABLECOINS OUTSIDE THE US (interactive lens). Mechanisms (well argued): deposits that fund lending can leave, monetary policy weakens, capital controls are harder to enforce. Measured so far (small): inflows move short-dated Treasury yields a few basis points; the IMF found no clear drain on bank deposits in El Salvador, a weak test because it already uses the dollar. Scenarios (large): one bank's research puts possible emerging-market deposit outflows at $1tn by 2028.

10. A UK BANK'S OPTIONS. UK cryptoasset regulations made 4 Feb 2026 and FCA final rules published 30 Jun 2026 both apply from 25 October 2027; firms already operating must apply between 30 Sep 2026 and 28 Feb 2027. The Bank of England will supervise sterling stablecoins the Treasury recognises as systemic; its 22 June 2026 policy replaced proposed holding limits with a temporary £40bn issuance cap per systemic coin and backing of up to 70% short-dated gilts with the rest in unremunerated Bank of England deposits (up to 95% gilts while scaling). Its rules are a draft due to be finalised by end-2026; no coin has been recognised. Draft legislation would take payments in UK-issued stablecoins out of the dealing and arranging rules; overseas coins such as USDT and USDC would stay inside them; a Treasury proposal would bring stablecoin payments into payments law, admitting overseas coins only if their home regime gives similar outcomes. Roles: tokenised deposits are live under existing law; issuing a sterling stablecoin needs FCA permission from Oct 2027 and a separate entity; custody and buying/selling for clients need registration now and FCA permission from Oct 2027; sending payments with third-party coins is the least settled area; staying out is legitimate. Options depend on need: tokenised deposits for 24/7 settlement between clients (JPMorgan, Citi in seven markets, HSBC in five already run them); partner with a licensed payout provider for corridors banks have left or suppliers wanting dollar tokens; distribution income after authorisation; issuing only via a separate entity with constrained economics; or wait. Alternatives are meant to narrow the gap: Faster Payments runs 24/7; more than 25 banks committed to Swift's faster retail rules by June 2026 (no volumes reported); Nexus is targeted for 2027 and not live; BIS Project Agora showed atomic cross-currency settlement is achievable.

KNOWN UNKNOWNS: whether the UK amending regulations have been made; the Bank of England's final code; the Treasury's payments-law response; real prices for a £1,000 UK payment; the IMF paper's full text; the McKinsey estimate's own page (read via BIS and IMF citations); Open USD partner payouts; local rules for receiving crypto-routed payments in any specific country, which the page does not assert.

RELATED TOPICS ON THE SITE: Stablecoin market structure (issuer-by-issuer detail), Deposit tokens, GBTD tokenised deposits, Regulation, What actually moves.

scenes.journey:
FOLLOW £1,000 SCENE. A £1,000 invoice, payable in the supplier’s local currency from a uk small business with a business account at a uk bank to a supplier abroad with an ordinary local bank account. "Paid" means the supplier holds what it asked for: local currency in its bank, or dollar tokens in its wallet. All amounts are shown as £-equivalent at the mid-market rate, so fees and spreads are comparable without quoting any live exchange rate. Prices are illustrative and identical per leg type, so only structure differs; the comparison view is not ranked.
ROUTE Bank transfer through correspondents: The UK bank sends a SWIFT message and settles across accounts it holds with a correspondent bank. Steps: 1) Bank takes the instruction and debits the business; 2) A SWIFT message instructs the correspondent; 3) The correspondent pays the supplier’s bank; 4) The supplier’s bank checks and credits the account. Strongest version: The bank has a direct correspondent in the destination, sends in local currency, and both banks process gpi payments promptly. Watch: Cut-offs, each bank in the chain may deduct a charge, and returns can take days if details are wrong. Big-bank retail wires can carry FX margins of 2–4%, even on liquid currencies.
ROUTE Payment firm with local accounts: A licensed payment firm takes pounds in the UK and pays out of local-currency money it already holds in the destination. Steps: 1) The business pays the firm by Faster Payments; 2) The firm converts and instructs a local payout; 3) Domestic payout to the supplier. Strongest version: The firm holds enough local currency in the destination and the destination has an instant domestic payment system. Watch: The firm must keep money parked in every currency it serves and move it back and forth in bulk. Corridors it doesn’t serve are unreachable.
ROUTE Stablecoin sandwich through a provider: A provider turns pounds into a dollar stablecoin, moves it on a blockchain to a partner, and the partner pays local currency. Steps: 1) The business pays the provider by Faster Payments; 2) The provider swaps pounds for a dollar stablecoin; 3) The tokens move on the blockchain; 4) The partner swaps the stablecoins for local currency; 5) Domestic payout to the supplier. Strongest version: The provider holds stablecoin inventory, its off-ramp partner is licensed and funded in local currency, and the destination has an instant domestic system. Watch: Two currency conversions, two partners and two prefunded balances. The token arriving does not pay the supplier.
ROUTE Wallet to wallet: The business buys a dollar stablecoin on an exchange and sends it to the supplier’s wallet. The supplier converts it themselves. Steps: 1) The business funds an exchange account; 2) The business buys a dollar stablecoin; 3) The exchange sends the tokens to the supplier’s wallet; 4) The supplier sells the tokens for local currency [only when local currency is needed]; 5) The supplier withdraws to their bank [only when local currency is needed]. Strongest version: The supplier already uses a licensed local exchange, wants dollars or can convert them cheaply, and both exchanges exchange Travel Rule data. Watch: The last two steps, and their cost and legal treatment, fall on the supplier. Without a wallet the route doesn’t start.
SITUATION CONTROLS: what the supplier needs (local currency or dollar tokens); whether banks and payment firms serve the corridor; supplier wallet (none or at an exchange); licensed off-ramp (funded, short of cash, none); destination payout system (instant 24/7 or banking hours); when sent (Tue 10:00, Fri 18:00, Sat 11:00); screening (clear or possible match). Presets: Corridor with licensed off-ramps: Banks and payment firms serve the corridor, licensed off-ramps are funded, and the destination has an instant domestic payment system. The supplier wants local currency in the bank. Bank-account-only supplier, no verified off-ramp: The supplier has a bank account and no stablecoin wallet, and no licensed crypto off-ramp is established for this flow. Local rules on receiving payments through crypto are not assumed. Corridor banks have left: Correspondent banks and payment firms have withdrawn from the corridor ("de-risking"), but a licensed off-ramp operates there. This is where stablecoin routes can reach payees banks no longer reach. Supplier wants dollar tokens: The supplier invoices in dollars and wants dollar stablecoins in its exchange wallet, for example to pay its own suppliers. Arrival of the tokens is the payment.
RULES: A sender checks prerequisites before anything moves. No supplier wallet: the wallet route can't start. No licensed off-ramp: a provider can't offer the sandwich. Banks withdrawn: the bank and payment-firm routes can't start. Dollar-token objective: bank routes can't deliver (they pay accounts, not wallets), the sandwich isn't needed, and wallet to wallet completes when the tokens arrive. An off-ramp short of cash makes the payout wait after the token arrives. Banking-hours payout systems make evening and weekend payouts wait; bank cut-offs delay the correspondent route. A possible screening match holds every route.
WHAT TO NOTICE: on the sandwich the tokens reach the off-ramp partner at step 3 of 5; the supplier holds nothing until step 5. With the default illustrative prices the sandwich matches the payment firm's cost only if each of its two conversions costs about half of the firm's single conversion (about 0.25% against 0.5%); dollar against major-currency spreads can be that tight, exotic currencies usually aren't.
scenes.routes:
PAYMENT-MODEL SELECTOR SCENE. Inputs: who pays (business, person, bank treasury); what the payee can receive into (bank, wallet, both); what it needs (local currency, dollars); what the payer starts with (bank money, stablecoins); whether both use the same platform or bank network; whether it must complete overnight or at a weekend; whether banks and payment firms serve the corridor; whether licensed crypto off-ramps exist. Results group models as Fits, Fits if, Doesn't fit.
MODEL Bank transfer through correspondents (bank-rails): SWIFT message plus settlement across nostro and vostro accounts. Prerequisites: Payee has a bank account; Banks in the chain process within their hours. Controls: Each bank screens; gpi tracking; returns through the same chain. Fails when: Wrong details trigger slow returns; cut-offs push payments to the next business day.
MODEL Payment firm with local accounts (bank-rails): Pounds in at home, prefunded local currency out at the destination. Prerequisites: The firm serves this corridor; Payee has a bank account; The firm holds enough local currency. Controls: The firm screens and monitors; safeguarding of client money at home. Fails when: The corridor isn’t served, or the firm’s local balance runs dry before it rebalances.
MODEL Linked instant payment systems (bank-rails): Two countries’ instant payment systems connected, so a domestic-style payment crosses the border. Prerequisites: A live link between the two countries; Both banks participate; The amount is within the link’s limits. Controls: Each side screens under its own rules; limits per transaction. Fails when: No link exists for the corridor, or the payment exceeds its limits.
MODEL Provider-managed stablecoin settlement (stablecoin): Fiat in, stablecoin across, fiat out. The customer never holds a token. Prerequisites: A licensed, funded off-ramp in the destination; Stablecoin inventory or issuer access; Local rules allow the off-ramp to pay out. Controls: Provider screens at entry; wallet screening and Travel Rule between providers; off-ramp screens at payout. Fails when: No licensed off-ramp, a dry local float, or a closed payout system. The token can arrive while the payee still has nothing.
MODEL Payment firm settling its own treasury leg in stablecoins (stablecoin): The customer sees an ordinary fiat payment. Behind it, the firm moves its own liquidity between countries in stablecoins. Prerequisites: The firm serves this corridor; Payee has a bank account; The firm can mint, buy and sell stablecoins at both ends. Controls: Customer controls are the firm’s usual ones. The token leg adds wallet custody, issuer exposure and reconciliation between the firm’s own entities. Fails when: The corridor isn’t served, or ramps at either end close or widen just when the firm needs to rebalance.
MODEL Exchange wallet to exchange wallet (stablecoin): Tokens move on-chain between accounts at two licensed exchanges or custodians. Prerequisites: Payee has a custodial wallet; Both providers exchange Travel Rule data; Payee is content to hold dollars, or converts them. Controls: Both providers screen; Travel Rule data passes with the transfer; blockchain analytics on the addresses. Fails when: The payee has no wallet, needs local currency in a bank, or the receiving provider can’t accept the Travel Rule data.
MODEL Self-custody wallet to wallet (stablecoin): Tokens move to or from a wallet whose owner controls the keys, with no provider in between. Prerequisites: Proof the payee owns the wallet; Analytics on the address and its history; The payer’s policy allows it. Controls: Ownership proof, wallet screening, enhanced due diligence, limits. Travel Rule data has no counterparty provider to go to. Fails when: Ownership can’t be shown, the address carries risk, or keys are lost. Transfers are irreversible.
MODEL Transfer inside one platform (stablecoin): Both parties hold accounts at the same exchange or custodian, which moves the balance on its own books. Prerequisites: Both parties are customers of the same provider. Controls: The provider screens both sides and keeps the records. Fails when: The provider fails. Both parties are exposed to the same custodian.
MODEL Tokenised deposits on a bank network (bank-token): Bank deposits recorded as tokens, moved between clients of one bank or a shared bank platform. Prerequisites: Both parties bank on the same network; The network operates at the hours needed. Controls: Ordinary bank KYC, sanctions and monitoring. The token is still the bank’s deposit liability. Fails when: The payee banks outside the network.
MODEL Mint and redeem with the issuer (stablecoin): An institution sends dollars to the issuer for new tokens, or returns tokens for dollars. Prerequisites: An onboarded account with the issuer; Issuer and US banking hours; Minimum sizes. Controls: The issuer’s onboarding and screening; the institution’s own controls. Fails when: Outside banking hours, or for anyone without an issuer account. It is a funding and cash-out tool, not a route to a third party.
MODEL Moving between blockchains (stablecoin): Issuer burn-and-mint, a bridge, a pool, or a provider paying out on the other chain. Prerequisites: Know which chain the payee’s wallet is on; Prefer the issuer’s own mechanism where it exists. Controls: Track the transfer to finality on both chains; keep it in transit on the books until then. Fails when: Confirmation is delayed, a bridge is exploited, a pool runs short, or a timeout tempts someone to send again.
scenes.liquidity:
LIQUIDITY CONTROL ROOM SCENE. A payout provider must pay 6 supplier invoices (P1 £40k, P2 £25k, P3 £60k, P4 £30k, P5 £50k, P6 £35k) between Friday 14:00 and Monday 09:00 through a dollar-stablecoin corridor; its off-ramp partner pays local currency. Amounts are illustrative £k-equivalent.
ASSUMED HOURS: UK bank FX and wire desks: assumed open Friday 14:00 and Monday 09:00 only. Faster Payments runs all the time. Issuer minting and redemption: assumed to follow US banking hours (09:00–16:00 New York), so open on Friday afternoon UK time and closed at weekends and early Monday UK time. Destination banks: assumed 5 hours ahead of the UK, so closed from Friday evening local time until Monday morning local time.
LEVERS: partner's local float (low £50k, medium £120k, high £300k); provider's stablecoin inventory (low £60k, high £300k); flows one way or both ways (both ways nets £40k on Saturday and Sunday); market makers normal (0.3% spread), stressed (3% and £30k per slot) or gone; direct mint/redeem account or none; payout system instant or banking hours; a £100k credit line or none.
MODEL: double-entry; balances never go negative unless the credit line is on, and borrowing is labelled as credit. Each invoice goes collected (customer debited), tokens with partner, money set aside (reserved), paid (spendable). LESSONS: thin float with no market maker, no issuer access and no credit leaves tokens with the partner and invoices unpaid; a banking-hours payout system means nothing is paid before Monday; flows in both directions let the provider net without converting; generous prefunding pays everything but leaves money parked; credit and spreads have costs.
scenes.crossledger:
CROSS-LEDGER FAILURE LAB SCENE. A bank holds 100,000 dollar stablecoins on Chain A and must pay a recipient on Chain B. The reader picks a method and a fault and steps through events; balances on each chain and the bank's books (treasury, in transit, paid, claim on a third party) always total 100,000.
METHOD Issuer burn and mint: The issuer’s own protocol destroys tokens on Chain A and, on its signed confirmation, creates the same amount on Chain B. Recipient ends up holding: The issuer’s own token on Chain B. Same claim, same issuer. Trusts: The issuer’s attestation service and contracts on both chains. Faults available: Confirmation is slow, Chain B transaction fails, Chain A reorganises, Timeout: outcome unknown, Recipient blocked.
METHOD Lock-and-mint bridge: A bridge locks the tokens in its contract on Chain A and mints its own wrapped token on Chain B. Recipient ends up holding: The bridge’s wrapped token: a claim on the bridge’s locked tokens, not on the issuer. Trusts: The bridge’s validators, its code and the safety of its locked funds. Faults available: Confirmation is slow, Chain B transaction fails, Chain A reorganises, Timeout: outcome unknown, Bridge is exploited.
METHOD Liquidity-pool bridge: The bank deposits into a pool on Chain A, and a pool on Chain B releases the same token from its own liquidity. Recipient ends up holding: The issuer’s token on Chain B, released from the pool. Trusts: The pool’s messaging layer and code, and enough liquidity waiting on Chain B. Faults available: Confirmation is slow, Chain A reorganises, Timeout: outcome unknown, Pool runs short.
METHOD Provider pays on Chain B: The bank sends tokens to a provider on Chain A. The provider pays the recipient from its own inventory on Chain B. Recipient ends up holding: The issuer’s token on Chain B, from the provider’s inventory. Trusts: The provider: its solvency, its controls and its inventory on Chain B. Faults available: Timeout: outcome unknown, Provider fails, Recipient blocked.
SAFE ACTIONS: rebroadcast the same signed transaction after a reorg (same nonce: at most one is included); look up a transaction by hash after a timeout, never send again; keep checking status when confirmation is slow; resubmit the same signed message after a failed mint (one-time identifier: can't mint twice); wait or use the documented refund when a pool is short. STOP: recipient blocked (escalate to compliance and the issuer; routing around a block is evasion); bridge drained (record the loss exposure; no retry fixes it); provider fails (credit exposure; lodge a claim). The payment is marked paid only after Chain B is final. A wrapped token is a claim on the bridge, not the issuer.
scenes.peg:
PEG SCENE ("two prices").
Redemption open, reserves trusted: Very close to $1.00. Holders who can redeem get $1 from the issuer, and new tokens are issued for $1. If the market price dips, they buy below $1 and redeem at $1. If it rises, they mint at $1 and sell. That trade holds the price.
Redemption open, reserves doubted: A discount, for as long as doubt lasts. Holders who can redeem rush to, and others sell. If the reserves are really there and redemption works, the price comes back. In March 2023, with $3.3bn of USDC’s reserves at the failed Silicon Valley Bank, USDC fell to about $0.88 and recovered once US authorities protected SVB’s depositors.
Redemption closed, reserves trusted: Can slip a little below $1. With redemption shut, at a weekend, on a bank holiday or during an issuer pause, the arbitrage can’t complete. Small discounts can open and stay until redemption reopens.
Redemption closed, reserves doubted: The deepest discount. No way to redeem and fear of loss together. The SVB episode ran over a weekend, when some exchanges paused conversion. Where nothing real backs the coin at all, as with the algorithmic TerraUSD in May 2022, there is no $1 to arbitrage towards.
Holder who can only sell: You get the market price. Par redemption protects only holders who can use it, directly or through someone who can. Most people sell on an exchange.
scenes.volume:
VOLUME SCENE (flows, 2025, one linear scale).
Stablecoin transfers on-chain, 2025 (gross): $28tn to $35tn (Estimates). Every transfer counted, including exchanges, trading bots, DeFi and transfers between a holder’s own wallets.
Visa payments volume, fiscal 2025: $14.2tn (Reported). A card network’s payments, for scale. A like-for-like payments figure.
Genuine stablecoin payments, 2025: $390bn (Estimates). McKinsey and Artemis estimate genuine payments (business, person-to-person, card-linked) at about this level. The BIS gives a similar figure for transfers net of moves between a holder’s own wallets, citing Chainalysis and Visa data.
of which business-to-business: $226bn (Same estimate). About 60% of the genuine-payment estimate.
Cross-border stablecoin transfers Chainalysis can attribute, year to June 2026: $220bn (Vendor lower bound). Only transfers it can attribute to countries. Not all are payments. The average transfer is about $3,000.
Stock, not flow: $286.4bn in circulation on 17 November 2026.
scenes.controls:
CONTROLS SCENE. A long-standing corporate client asks its UK bank to pay a supplier in a dollar stablecoin; the checks depend on the destination wallet.
Wallet at a licensed exchange: Proceed with documented checks. Can infer: Which exchange holds it, and in which country. Whether that exchange can exchange Travel Rule data. Cannot infer: Who controls the key, or on whose behalf. That today’s “low risk” score is right. Labels are probabilistic and often added late. Do: Send Travel Rule data with the transfer (in the UK, full originator data at or above £800). Screen the supplier’s name and the exchange. Keep the evidence.
Self-custody wallet, long clean history: Defensible with purpose, address confirmation and monitoring. Can infer: When the address was first funded, and who it has dealt with. Whether analytics link it to known services. Cannot infer: Who controls the key, or on whose behalf. That today’s “low risk” score is right. Labels are probabilistic and often added late. Do: Ask the client for the supplier’s identity, contract and reason for using this address. If the bank sends from its own custody and asks for Travel Rule information it doesn’t get, it must not make the transfer. Confirm the address with a known contact through a separate channel. At higher values, ask for proof of control: a signed message or a small test transfer. It proves control of a key, not who owns the business.
Newly created wallet: Hold: enhanced checks and a staged payment before release. Can infer: That there is no history. That is not evidence either way. Cannot infer: Anything about its owner or purpose. Who controls the key, or on whose behalf. That today’s “low risk” score is right. Labels are probabilistic and often added late. Do: Treat a large first transfer to a new wallet as a red flag, as OFSI does. Get proof of control and confirm the address through a known contact. Requested information that never arrives means no transfer. Send a test amount first, apply limits, and monitor afterwards.
Analytics flag: sanctions exposure: Stop. Don’t pay; report. Can infer: Direct or indirect exposure to listed addresses within the hops screened. Cannot infer: Whether indirect exposure means the supplier is a designated person. That needs analysis of the path. Do: If the address is listed or reasonably suspected to be controlled by a designated person, do not make the payment. Freeze related assets the bank holds and report to OFSI. File a SAR with the NCA where laundering is suspected. Record the attribution reasoning either way.
Analytics flag: scam or mule exposure, or details recently changed: Stop and verify: treat it as possible invoice redirection. Can infer: Exposure to known scam clusters, or a pattern typical of mule accounts. Cannot infer: Whether the real supplier changed its details or someone is impersonating it. Do: Stop and verify with the supplier through known contacts, not those on the invoice. Consider a SAR. If paying would itself be a money-laundering offence, ask the NCA for consent and wait. Don’t rely on the issuer to freeze it later: freezes miss value that has already moved.
Before sending: Know the customer and the payment (catches named sanctioned or unknown parties; a business reason that doesn’t add up. Misses who actually controls the destination address.); Attribute and screen the address (catches listed addresses and exposure to sanctioned, mixer, theft or scam clusters, at least 3–5 hops back. Misses new addresses, clusters not yet labelled, cross-chain hops.); Exchange Travel Rule data (catches missing or mismatched names when the other side is a crypto business. Misses unhosted wallets, and counterparties where the rule isn’t enforced.); Confirm the address another way (catches lookalike addresses and invoice redirection. Misses a compromised approval process.)
At release: Rescreen at release (catches listings added since onboarding. Misses labels that arrive after the transaction is broadcast.); Signing controls (catches unauthorised or altered withdrawals. Misses compromised devices or people around the keys.); Issuer blocking (catches transfers to or from addresses the issuer has already frozen. Misses addresses not yet frozen, and value already swapped into other assets.)
After sending: Monitor and look back (catches later attribution and onward flows to risky services. Misses cash-outs through informal desks. often the funds have gone.); Report (catches produces the intelligence behind freezes: sars to the nca, reports to ofsi. Misses doesn’t stop movement itself.); Freeze and seize (catches tokens still sitting in identified wallets. Misses value already swapped, bridged or used as collateral.)
scenes.reserve:
RESERVE ECONOMICS SCENE: four ways to put a dollar on a ledger.
Single issuer: Examples: USDC (Circle in the US, its French e-money subsidiary in the EU), USDT (Tether), PYUSD (Paxos, for PayPal), RLUSD (Ripple) | Who owes the holder: The issuing company, or its entity for the holder’s region. Distributors and exchanges owe the holder nothing on the token. | What backs it: Reserves held for holders: Treasury bills, repo, money-market funds and cash. Tether also reports gold and bitcoin. | Who earns the income: The issuer, minus what it pays distributors. In Q3 2026 Circle earned $658m of reserve income and paid $409m in distribution and transaction costs. | What the holder gets: No interest from the issuer. Some platforms pay rewards from their own share, which is the open question in the US. | Who can redeem, and how: Onboarded customers, directly. Tether: $100,000 minimum and a fee of the greater of $1,000 or 0.1%. Everyone else sells in the market. | Reach: Any wallet on any supported chain, subject to freezes.
Revenue-sharing network: Examples: USDG on the Global Dollar Network (issued by Paxos); Open USD (issued by Bridge, part of Stripe; live since 30 Sep 2026) | Who owes the holder: The issuer (Paxos or Bridge), not the partners who distribute it. | What backs it: Reserves held by the issuer for holders. | Who earns the income: Shared with distributors. Paxos offers partners up to 100% of the returns on USDG held on their platforms. Open USD says partners earn rewards in proportion to the supply they drive, but no payouts or fees have been published. | What the holder gets: No interest from the issuer. Partners may pass rewards on. | Who can redeem, and how: Through the issuer and onboarded partners. | Reach: Wherever partners distribute it. Open USD’s supply was about $961m on 17 November 2026.
Bank-issued stablecoin: Examples: EURCV and USDCV (SG-FORGE, a Société Générale subsidiary; e-money tokens under MiCA); SoFiUSD (issued by SoFi Bank itself) | Who owes the holder: The issuing bank or bank subsidiary, against segregated reserves rather than its deposit book. In the UK the PRA expects a separate, insolvency-remote, distinctly branded entity. | What backs it: Segregated reserves, not the bank’s loan book. | Who earns the income: The banking group keeps the reserve income. | What the holder gets: No interest under MiCA, GENIUS or the UK rules. | Who can redeem, and how: At par, on the regime’s terms. MiCA: at any time. | Reach: Any wallet on supported chains, like any stablecoin.
Tokenised deposit: Examples: JPM Coin (JPMorgan Kinexys), Citi Token Services, HSBC Tokenised Deposit Service, the UK GBTD pilots | Who owes the holder: The bank itself. It is the bank’s ordinary deposit liability, recorded as a token. | What backs it: The bank’s balance sheet, capital and liquidity, with deposit protection where the holder is eligible. | Who earns the income: The bank, as with any deposit: it lends against it. It may pay interest. | What the holder gets: What any depositor gets, including interest if the bank pays it. | Who can redeem, and how: It is already the bank’s money. Moving it out is an ordinary payment. | Reach: Clients of that bank or of the banks on the shared network.
scenes.lens:
ECONOMY LENS SCENE: gains and costs of dollar stablecoins by perspective. Labels: measured, mechanism, scenario, rule.
Economy with an unstable currency / Household or firm: gains [mechanism] Round-the-clock access to dollars without a US bank account. [measured] Some corridors are cheaper: the IMF found about 2% for a USD 200 stablecoin transfer with the cheapest ramps and 3% with typical ones, against 6.2% on average across traditional providers and 3.0% for the cheapest three. Costs [rule] No interest from the issuer: banned under MiCA now and under the GENIUS Act from January 2027. The issuer keeps the yield on the reserves. [measured] In about a third of comparable corridors the cheapest traditional provider was cheaper. [mechanism] No deposit protection, exposure to the issuer and to freezes, and local legal uncertainty.
Economy with an unstable currency / Local bank: gains [mechanism] Can earn fees by offering access, custody or payouts. Costs [mechanism] Dollar deposits that fund lending can move out into stablecoins, tightening domestic credit. [measured] Measured so far: the IMF found no clear disintermediation in El Salvador. That country already uses the dollar, so it is a weak test. [scenario] One bank’s research puts possible emerging-market deposit outflows at about USD 1tn by 2028. That is a scenario, not a measurement.
Economy with an unstable currency / Central bank: gains [measured] Remittances can arrive faster and cheaper in some corridors. Costs [mechanism] Faster dollarisation, weaker monetary-policy transmission, and capital controls that are "likely to be imperfect". [mechanism] Flows are hard to see: no single jurisdiction can assess global stablecoin arrangements fully.
Economy with an unstable currency / US issuer: gains [mechanism] Reserve income on Treasury bills, with no interest to pay holders. [measured] Inflows push down short-dated Treasury yields slightly: about 4 basis points within 10 days for a USD 3.5bn inflow. Costs [policy] Expected to be able to freeze, block and report on request, in every jurisdiction where its tokens circulate. [mechanism] Exposure to sanctions and illicit-finance enforcement in markets it doesn’t control.
The UK / Household or firm: gains [measured] Little gain for ordinary sterling payments: Faster Payments already settles in seconds, 24/7. [mechanism] Dollar exposure and crypto-market access for those who want them. Costs [policy] No deposit protection. The UK stablecoin regime does not apply until 25 October 2027.
The UK / Local bank: gains [mechanism] Custody, distribution and tokenised-deposit services for clients. Costs [policy] Deposits that leave reduce lending capacity. That is why the Bank of England plans to cap each systemic sterling stablecoin at £40bn to start. [policy] The PRA expects a bank to issue stablecoins only from a separate, insolvency-remote, distinctly branded entity.
The UK / Central bank: gains [policy] A regulated sterling stablecoin could serve tokenised markets, such as settlement in the Digital Securities Sandbox. Costs [policy] Credit supply during the transition. Hence a planned temporary £40bn guardrail and 70/30 backing in short gilts and Bank of England deposits.
The UK / US issuer: gains [policy] Yield on up to 70% of backing held in short-dated gilts, and up to 95% while scaling. Costs [policy] 30% of backing in unremunerated Bank of England deposits, no interest to holders, and a £40bn issuance cap. [policy] Redemption at par: within 24 hours for systemic coins, and T+1 after checks under the FCA rules.
scenes.check:
SCENARIO CHECKS: eight new situations. Explain the reasoning; do not just give the letter.
1. On a Saturday your dollar stablecoin trades at $0.97 on an exchange. The issuer says reserves are complete, and redemption with the issuer reopens on Monday. What is the most likely explanation? Best answer: Arbitrage can’t run until redemption reopens, so a small discount can persist. If reserves are really there, redeemers close the gap. Why: Yes. The peg is held by people who can redeem at $1. Shut that door and small gaps can stay open.
2. A token lands in a supplier’s wallet five seconds after a UK business presses send. Has the supplier been paid? Best answer: Only if dollar tokens are what the supplier wanted. If it needs local currency in its bank, it isn’t paid until an off-ramp pays out. Why: Right. “Paid” means the payee holds what it needs. The token can be the whole payment or one leg of it.
3. A UK business must pay an invoice to a supplier in India. The supplier has a bank account and no stablecoin wallet. What should the business’s bank recommend? Best answer: A fiat payout route: a bank transfer, a payment firm, or a stablecoin provider only if it has a licensed partner that can lawfully pay rupees into the account. Check that, don’t assume it. Why: Yes. The route must end in the supplier’s bank account, and reachability and local rules for crypto-routed payments must be checked, not assumed.
4. A bank burned 100,000 USDC on Chain A using the issuer’s burn-and-mint protocol. The burn is final, but the mint on Chain B failed during congestion. What is safe to do? Best answer: Resubmit the same signed message on Chain B. It can mint only once. Why: Yes. Each message has a one-time identifier, so a retry can’t pay twice. Keep the 100,000 in transit on the books until Chain B is final.
5. A supplier must have local currency in its bank account by Sunday evening. The tokens reached the off-ramp partner on Saturday, but the issuer’s redemption window is closed until Monday. Which statement is right? Best answer: The partner can still pay from local currency it already holds, sell the tokens to a market maker at a spread, or draw on credit. Otherwise the payout waits for Monday. Why: Yes. Prefunding, market makers and credit are the levers. Each has a cost: money parked, a spread, or borrowing.
6. A long-standing corporate client asks its UK bank to pay a supplier in stablecoins. The destination wallet was created yesterday, and analytics score it “low risk”. What should the bank do? Best answer: Treat a large first transfer to a new wallet as a red flag: confirm the address through a known contact, get proof of control, stage the payment and keep records. Stop and report if sanctions links appear. Why: Yes. Proportionate, documented checks, with escalation if anything is found.
7. In a country with high inflation, households move savings from local bank deposits into dollar stablecoins. Which statement is best supported? Best answer: Households gain dollar access. Banks lose deposits that fund lending, and monetary policy may weaken. These are mechanisms; measured effects so far are small, and the large numbers are scenarios. Why: Yes, and keep the labels: mechanism, measured or scenario. In the UK the same worry is why the Bank of England caps systemic sterling coins.
8. A bank’s strategy paper treats four instruments as interchangeable: a single-issuer stablecoin, a coin on a revenue-sharing network, a stablecoin from the bank’s own separate subsidiary, and the bank’s tokenised deposit. Which correction is right? Best answer: The tokenised deposit is the bank’s own deposit. The subsidiary’s coin is a claim on a separate issuer. Network partners earn reserve income but owe the holder nothing. The single issuer keeps the income minus distribution costs. Why: Yes. Separate the token issuer, the distributor, the bank liability and the redemption right.
